glossary.Spinal cord compression: Pressure on the spinal cord from a mass, bleed, disc or infection that stops it working below that level.
glossary.Lumbosacral nerve roots: The nerve roots leaving the lower spine (lumbar and sacral) that supply the legs, bladder and bowel.
glossary.Paralysis: Loss of the ability to move a muscle or limb.
glossary.Sphincter dysfunction: Loss of control of the bladder or bowel outlet muscles.
glossary.Metastatic: Cancer that has spread from where it started to another site.
glossary.Thoracic: The middle section of the spine, attached to the ribs.
glossary.Red flags: Symptoms or signs that point to a serious cause and need urgent action.
glossary.Spinal tenderness: Pain when pressing over the spine, suggesting a local problem such as infection or tumour.
glossary.Band-like: Pain encircling the trunk at one level, like a tight belt, from a compressed thoracic nerve root.
glossary.Faecal incontinence: Loss of control of the bowels.
glossary.Sexual dysfunction: Problems with sexual function, such as erectile dysfunction, from nerve damage.
glossary.UMN signs: Signs of damage above the anterior horn cell: brisk reflexes, spasticity, weakness, upgoing plantars.
glossary.Upper motor neurone: The nerve cell running from the brain down the spinal cord to the anterior horn.
glossary.L1: The first lumbar vertebra, roughly where the spinal cord ends in adults.
glossary.Ankle jerks: The ankle reflex: tapping the Achilles tendon makes the foot point down.
glossary.Plantar responses: Foot reflex from stroking the sole; toes normally go down, upgoing toes mean a UMN lesion.
glossary.Spinal disc herniation: The soft centre of an intervertebral disc bulging out and pressing on a nerve root.
glossary.S1: The first sacral segment, just below L5.
glossary.Anticoagulation: Blood-thinning drugs, such as warfarin or DOACs, that reduce clotting.
glossary.AF: Atrial fibrillation: an irregular heart rhythm, often treated with anticoagulants.
glossary.Iatrogenic: Caused by medical treatment or a procedure.
glossary.Epidural analgesia: Pain relief given through a catheter into the epidural space, for example in labour.
glossary.MRI: Magnetic resonance imaging; the best scan for showing the spinal cord and soft tissue.
glossary.Neurosurgery: The specialty that operates on the brain and spine.
glossary.Prophylactically: Given in advance to prevent a problem rather than treat it.
glossary.Peptic ulceration: Ulcers in the stomach or duodenum, made more likely by steroids.
glossary.Stabilisation: Getting a patient settled and safe before definitive treatment.
glossary.Escalation: Calling for more senior help or a higher level of care.
glossary.Mobility: The ability to move about and walk.
glossary.Conus medullaris syndrome: Compression of the tapered end of the cord at L1, giving mixed upper and lower motor neurone signs.
glossary.Lower motor neurone: The nerve running from the anterior horn of the cord out to the muscle.
glossary.Vertebral body: The thick, weight-bearing front block of each vertebra.
glossary.Venous congestion: Pooling of blood in veins because drainage is blocked.
glossary.Mechanical compression: Direct physical squashing of a structure.
glossary.Spinal canal: The bony tunnel through the vertebrae that contains the spinal cord.
glossary.Ischaemic: Damaged by lack of blood supply.
glossary.Decompression: Relieving pressure on the cord, usually by surgically removing what is pressing on it.
glossary.Steroids: Corticosteroid drugs such as dexamethasone that reduce swelling and inflammation.
